newsitem.title: USA: IBM to announce network computer division.
newsitem.headline: IBM to announce network computer division.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. is expected to announce Monday that it is forming a new division focused on developing network computers, the new breed of low-cost, scaled-down computers, industry sources said.

The world's largest computer maker, based in Armonk, N.Y., was the first computer firm to introduce one of the much-hyped devices - also known as NCs - which have no floppy disks, CD-ROM drives, or huge operating systems taking up disk space.
By creating the Network Computer unit, a division focused on the development and marketing of NCs, IBM is further endorsing the nascent market.

IBM is expected to announce that Robert Dies, currently the general manager of the AS/400 minicomputer division, will head up its Network Computer unit. Dies will report to Bob Stephenson, the head of IBM's Personal Systems business.
A spokesman for IBM declined to comment.
Network computers have captivated the attention of the computer industry, because they represent a challenge to the dominance of Microsoft Corp and Intel Corp.

They are also becoming a popular concept because of their low maintenance cost versus the PC. Several companies have said in recent weeks that one PC can cost a corporation $6,000 to $12,000 a year to maintain, between software upgrades, diagnostics and other necessary maintenance.

Network computers do not have huge operating systems such as Windows or big applications that use space on a hard disk drive and take up memory space. They have small operating systems and temporarily use applications software and access data over corporate networks and the Internet.

So far the current market is aimed at corporate users, who may begin to see NCs instead of desktop computers, hooked up to a network. NCs are not expected to replace PCs, but they are believed to take some share of the overall PC market.
IBM remains a major player in the PC business and it has no intention of abandoning one market for the other. "(IBM) wants to play in both markets," said one industry source.
IBM introduced its Network Station in September, aimed at the corporate market and priced at less than $700, without a monitor. The company will begin shipping in volume next month.

Two weeks ago, Sun Microsystems Inc, whose company mantra is "the network is the computer" introduced its first JavaStation, priced at $742, without a monitor or keyboard. And Oracle Corp, which has been evangelizing the concept of network computers for over a year, announced a new Network Computer last week, based around Intel's Pentium, and several manafacturing partners.

IBM's new business unit will enable the computer giant to coordinate all its network computer development, manufacturing and marketing efforts across the company, as it has done with its Internet division.
